chunks: "I split it into three buckets: get more signal, make the electronics quieter, and clean up in processing.

For more signal, noise in a camera is mostly photon shot noise, so you want more photons: a wider aperture, a longer exposure, bigger pixels or pixel binning, or combine many frames, which is what night mode does.
Averaging N frames gives a square-root-of-N improvement.

For quieter electronics, you want a low-read-noise sensor with correlated double sampling, a clean analog supply, a good layout so digital noise doesn't couple in, and keep the sensor cool because dark current doubles every few degrees.
Using the sensor's native low-gain mode, or its dual-conversion-gain mode, avoids amplifying noise.
Then there's calibration: fixed-pattern noise doesn't average away, so you subtract a dark frame, map out hot pixels and correct pixel-to-pixel gain with a flat field.
Finally, in the ISP, denoising: spatial filters like bilateral or non-local-means, temporal filtering across frames for video, and increasingly neural networks.
The trade-off is always detail: every filter that removes noise risks smoothing real texture, so you denoise chroma harder than luma and you do it before sharpening and on raw data when possible."
